extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/ethics (general educated readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative criteria and behavioural standards for moral character, love, and asceticism as presented by Schopenhauer — covering how justice, sympathy, pure love, and the denial of the will to live manifest in conduct (chastity, poverty, self-mortification, patience, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure love (αγαπη, caritas) is sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: All true and pure love is sympathy; love which is not sympathy is selfishness. Ερος is selfishness, αγαπη is sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer contrasts this with Kant (who reduces virtue to duty and abstract reflection). He notes that the tones and caresses of true love coincide with sympathy; Italian 'pietà' denotes both sympathy and true love. Anti-pattern: treating felt sympathy as weakness (Kant's view). Combinations occur (e.g., genuine friendship mixes selfish pleasure and sympathy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weeping as evidence of sympathy/goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: Weeping is not a direct expression of pain but 'sympathy with our own selves'—a reflection of imagined suffering and our sympathy for that imagined sufferer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weeping arises through imagination and self-commiseration; it depends on capacity for love and imagination. It disarms anger and is regarded as a sign of goodness. Examples and support: Petrarch's description; children often do not cry until someone commiserates them. When moved to tears by another's suffering, we put ourselves in their place or see the fate of humanity generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as partial penetration of the principium individuationis
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice proceeds from a lesser degree of penetration of the principium individuationis — a widening of interest beyond the self that treats accidents affecting individuals collectively as balanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an intermediate moral stage: interest extends to innumerable manifestations but not yet to full identification with others. It equalises concern for others' fortunes with one's own, reducing anxiety that stems from concentrated self-concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goodness/disinterested love arises from higher penetration
rubrics_metrics.description: When penetration of the principium individuationis is carried further, genuine goodness of disposition (disinterested love) arises: placing other individuals and their fate completely on a level with one's own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical sign: willingness to sacrifice one's own life or well-being for the welfare of many (examples: Codrus, Leonidas, Regulus, Decius Mus, Arnold von Winkelried; Socrates, Giordano Bruno as martyrs for truth). There is no reason to prefer another's individuality to one's own except when many outweigh the one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts of love alleviate suffering (suffering is essential to life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suffering is essential to life; wishes stem from need/suffering, and satisfaction is merely removal of pain. Therefore what goodness and love do for others is essentially alleviation of suffering, which proceeds from knowledge of others' suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: genuine moral action is motivated by empathy grounded in awareness of suffering. Joys are negative (end of pain), so virtue functions to reduce suffering rather than to produce positive happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine friendship mixes selfishness and sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship almost always includes both selfish pleasure in the friend's presence and sympathy expressed in sincere participation and disinterested sacrifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer cites Spinoza: benevolence arises from compassion. Anti-pattern: expecting pure disinterested friendship without any element of mutual pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: The denial of the will to live as the highest ethical outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Full penetration of the principium individuationis leads to recognition of the identity of will in all beings, producing a turning away from life: voluntary renunciation, resignation, indifference, and perfect will-lessness (denial of the will to live).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phenomenological sign: transition from virtue to asceticism; the moral ideal is not worldly conquest but the quiet life of one who subdues the will. Schopenhauer uses metaphors (path of hot coals) and scriptural images (camel through the eye of a needle) to show difficulty of sustaining renunciation in ordinary life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary and complete chastity as the first step in asceticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary and complete chastity denies the assertion of the will via sensual gratification and is the first practical step in the denial of the will to live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chastity is practiced to prevent further assertion of the will beyond the individual life. Schopenhauer acknowledges a natural implication (if universal, species would die out) but frames chastity as a moral mortification of the will rather than a biological prescription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary and intentional poverty as mortification of will
rubrics_metrics.description: Poverty, practised intentionally and as an end in itself, serves as a constant mortification of the will so that worldly comforts cannot reawaken desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish from accidental almsgiving: here poverty is chosen to prevent pleasures from nourishing the will. It is an ascetic practice paralleled across Christian and Hindu traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Welcoming suffering and returning good for evil
rubrics_metrics.description: One who denies the will gladly accepts suffering, injury, ignominy, and insult as confirmation of not asserting the will; he bears them with inexhaustible patience and meekness and returns good for evil without ostentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conduct demonstrates that the person no longer resists manifestations of the will in the body or in others. It is an ethical indicator of successful mortification of volition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mortification of the body through fasting, chastisement, and self-inflicted torture
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascetics deliberately weaken and mortify the body (fasting, chastisement, self-torture) to break down the will that finds expression in bodily vitality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices span a wide range of historical examples (Christian penitents, Hindu self-sacrifice such as starvation, throwing themselves under wheels, burial alive, flinging from precipices). The aim is not cruelty for its own sake but to prevent the body from reanimating desire and will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saintliness proven by conduct, not doctrinal correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: A saint's conduct alone certifies saintliness; it proceeds from inward knowledge and need not align with philosophic correctness or rational dogma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer observes that saints may hold superstitions or different dogmas, but their moral worth is shown in actions. Anti-pattern: demanding a moralist teach only the virtue he himself possesses (an unreasonable requirement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical versus intuitive knowledge: exemplification through lives
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy can express the denial of the will abstractly; but the intuitive knowledge from which ascetic conduct springs is best understood via concrete lives and biographies of saints and ascetics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To fully grasp denial of the will, study biographies and accounts (e.g., lives of St. Francis, Autobiography of Madame de Guion, Indian ascetics). Schopenhauer argues deeds and conduct are the perfect expression of this ethical state, more instructive than historical narratives of worldly events.

rubrics_metrics.name: The highest moral significance is the subduer, not the conqueror, of the world
rubrics_metrics.description: For the philosopher, the most significant phenomenon is the quiet life of the man who, by surrendering and denying the will to live, attains moral freedom—this is morally greater than worldly conquest or public glory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: History focuses on assertion of the will (conquerors, mass movements), but ethical valuation privileges individual renunciation and moral inwardness. Schopenhauer encourages attention to accounts of holy, self-denying lives for ethical insight.
